title: Bondi v. VanDerStok (2025)
summary: A weapon parts kit that ships with every part needed and can be finished in about twenty minutes with common tools is a “weapon” that “may readily be converted” to fire under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), so ATF’s 2022 rule reaching such kits is valid in at least some applications and survives a facial challenge; harder kits were left for later cases.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2025. Key line: "Really, the kit's name says it all: 'Buy Build Shoot.'" (Justice Gorsuch)

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the Attorney General (Bondi, substituted for Garland) and the federal officials responsible for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, defending ATF’s 2022 rule. The respondents were individual gun owners, at-home gunsmiths, firearm manufacturers and dealers, and allied organizations that brought a pre-enforcement challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act. Justice Gorsuch wrote for a seven-Justice majority on March 26, 2025; Justice Jackson concurred; Justice Thomas dissented, as did Justice Alito.
sections.Material Facts: Congress enacted the Gun Control Act of 1968 after finding that criminals could too easily obtain untraceable guns. Section 921(a)(3)(A) defines a firearm to include “any weapon (including a starter gun) which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile by the action of an explosive.” Sellers treated kits as outside the Act; “ghost guns” submitted for tracing rose from about 1,600 in 2017 to more than 19,000 in 2021. ATF’s 2022 rule read the definition to cover a kit designed to, or readily capable of being completed, assembled or converted to, expel a projectile. Kits vary widely: some omit essential parts and demand specialized skill, while Polymer80’s “Buy Build Shoot” kit contained every component of a Glock-variant pistol and, in an ATF test, a novice built a working gun in twenty-one minutes with common tools and YouTube instructions.
sections.Procedural History: Before enforcement began the respondents filed what they called a facial challenge under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C), arguing that the Act categorically excludes weapon parts kits so that the kit provision exceeded ATF’s authority. The Northern District of Texas agreed on summary judgment and vacated the rule, 680 F. Supp. 3d 741 (2023), and the Fifth Circuit largely affirmed, holding that no kit could ever satisfy the statutory definition regardless of completeness or ease of assembly, 86 F.4th 179. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on October 8, 2024, and reversed and remanded. Because the respondents never disputed the government’s account of their facial burden, one valid application of the rule was enough to defeat the challenge.
sections.Issue: Does § 921(a)(3)(A) authorize ATF to regulate at least some weapon parts kits as a “weapon” that “may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, defeating the respondents’ facial claim that ATF lacks authority over every kit? That breaks into whether an unassembled kit can be a weapon at all, whether such a kit may readily be converted to fire, and whether lenity or constitutional avoidance narrows the definition because the Act carries criminal penalties.
sections.Holding: Yes. The definition has two requirements, a “weapon” and one of three functional conditions, and some kits satisfy both. The Polymer80 kit is a weapon because its intended function as an instrument of combat is obvious even before assembly, and it may readily be converted to fire because finishing it takes no more time, effort, expertise or specialized tools than converting a starter gun, which the statute itself treats as a weapon. Since the respondents argued only that no kit could ever qualify, showing that some do defeats the facial challenge. Text, context and structure resolved the examples before the Court, so lenity and avoidance played no role; the classification of more incomplete or labor-intensive kits was reserved. Reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: But “weapon” is an artifact noun, one whose application follows the object’s intended human function, and ordinary speakers use such nouns for unfinished objects when the function is clear: an author’s unfinished novel, a boxed IKEA table awaiting assembly, a rifle disassembled for cleaning. Polymer80 supplied every necessary component, required about twenty minutes of ordinary work, and sold the product as “Buy Build Shoot”; its name says it all. Congress expressly included starter guns, which fire only blanks as sold and can be converted to live fire with a common power tool in under an hour. The starter gun also supplied the yardstick for “readily”: its conversion takes common tools, ordinary skill and less than an hour, and the Polymer80 kit demanded no more. A kit missing essential parts or requiring substantial time, specialized skill or uncommon equipment may fall outside both terms and could support as-applied challenges. Justice Thomas read “weapon” to require an existing instrument usable in combat, distinguished kits from disassembled rifles and starter guns because those have functional frames or receivers, and would have applied lenity to any ambiguity.

topics.lrs-k-textualism: The majority fixes the meaning of "weapon" as of 1968 with dictionaries and ordinary usage, treating the word as an artifact noun whose intended function can be clear before assembly.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The starter-gun parenthetical and the "designed to" and "readily converted" clauses are read together so that each clause does work, which is how the Court both defines "weapon" and calibrates "readily."
topics.lrs-k-lenity: Both the plaintiffs and the dissent invoke lenity because the Act carries criminal penalties, but the majority holds that lenity has no role where text, context, and structure decide the case.
topics.lrs-s-enabling-statute: ATF issued the rule under section 926(a), and Justice Jackson's concurrence frames the whole case as a question of whether the agency stayed within the boundaries Congress drew in section 921(a)(3).
topics.lrs-s-avoidance: The plaintiffs asked the Court to narrow the definition through constitutional avoidance, and the majority declined because avoidance applies only when the text is genuinely ambiguous.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Gorsuch wrote for a seven-Justice majority. Justice Jackson concurred, stressing that excess-of-authority review under 5 U.S.C. section 706(2)(C) asks only whether the agency crossed actual statutory boundaries, not whether judges would have made the same discretionary choices. Justices Sotomayor and Kavanaugh also concurred (opinions omitted from the excerpt). Justice Thomas dissented, arguing that a kit is not a "weapon" under the ordinary meaning of the word and that lenity should resolve any ambiguity; Justice Alito also dissented (omitted). The vote was 7 to 2.
learning.why: The case shows textualism at work on a definition: the majority builds its reading from a period dictionary, a linguistic observation about artifact nouns, and internal clues such as the starter-gun parenthetical, then refuses lenity and avoidance because text and structure already answer the question. It also shows how facial versus as-applied framing shapes what a court must decide.
